=== STEP 1: NUMBERED FACT LIST (source of truth: examples/field-guide/artifact/GUIDE.md) ===
Body split into sentences on '.', '!', '?'; every sentence stating a checkable fact indexed from F1. Headers excluded. 32 facts total.
F1  Guide prepares a household for a power outage lasting up to seventy-two hours.
F2  Written for a temperate climate and assumes no backup generator.
F3  Work through the sections in order; earlier sections cover the preparations that matter most.
F4  Store four litres of water per person per day = twelve litres per person for the full seventy-two hours.
F5  Half of that allowance is for drinking, the other half covers cooking and basic hygiene.
F6  Store water in food-grade containers, keep out of direct sunlight, replace stored water every six months.
F7  If a storm is forecast, also fill the bathtub; bathtub water is for flushing toilets and washing, never drinking.
F8  Keep a dedicated shelf of non-perishable food sufficient for three days.
F9  Good choices: canned beans, canned fish, peanut butter, crackers, dried fruit, shelf-stable milk.
F10 Choose foods that require no cooking, and own a manual can opener, because an electric one will be useless.
F11 Eat perishable refrigerator food first, then freezer food, and only then the emergency shelf.
F12 An unopened refrigerator keeps food safe for about four hours.
F13 A full freezer holds a safe temperature for about forty-eight hours, but a half-full freezer for only about twenty-four hours.
F14 Keep both doors closed as much as possible and tape a note to each door as a reminder.
F15 Any perishable food that has spent more than two hours above four degrees Celsius should be discarded.
F16 Use battery-powered LED lanterns or headlamps as primary light; avoid candles, a leading cause of house fires during outages.
F17 Store at least one light per person, plus two spare sets of batteries for each light.
F18 Keep one headlamp beside each bed and one lantern in the kitchen, placed where they can be found in the dark.
F19 Never run a camping stove, barbecue, or generator indoors/garage/near a window; each produces carbon monoxide, odourless and can be fatal.
F20 Install at least one battery-powered carbon monoxide alarm on each floor where people sleep.
F21 In cold weather, gather everyone in one small room on a south-facing side, close the door; layered clothing/blankets safer than any improvised heater.
F22 If the indoor temperature falls below ten degrees Celsius and you cannot maintain warmth, relocate to a warming centre or neighbour's home.
F23 Keep a battery-powered or hand-crank radio; know the frequency of your local emergency station before the outage begins.
F24 Charge every phone/power bank when a storm is forecast; a full 20000 mAh power bank recharges a typical phone roughly four times.
F25 Put phone in low-power mode at outage start; agree on one out-of-area contact everyone texts, as texts beat congested networks vs voice calls.
F26 Keep a first-aid kit and a seven-day supply of every prescription medication, rotated to stay in date.
F27 Refrigerated medication such as insulin generally stays usable at room temperature for up to twenty-eight days (confirm with pharmacist).
F28 Write pharmacy, doctor, and poison-control phone numbers on paper, because a dead phone is not a phone book.
F29 Wait five minutes before switching major appliances back on, so the grid can stabilise.
F30 Check the freezer: if food still contains ice crystals, it can be safely refrozen.
F31 Restock everything used within one week, starting with water and batteries.
F32 Write a one-page note on what was missing or awkward, and fix at least one gap before the next outage.
